metadata.title: The Experience of Middle-Income Countries Participating in PISA 2000-2015 (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This report synthesises evidence across PISA cycles and does not present a single student-level empirical ML model with a clearly specified analytic dataset and weight variables. Where PISA 2012 mathematics analyses are described (in the chapter on education quality and equity), the text states that multi-level models apply both school and student weights following standard OECD procedures, but the specific weight variable names are not provided in the excerpt. The report also discusses that PISA uses complex sampling and that comparability across countries is maintained through standardised procedures, implying the need for survey-weighted estimation when producing population-representative estimates. For replication, analysts should use the OECD/PISA technical documentation for the relevant cycle to identify the correct student and school weight variables and to apply them consistently with the multilevel modelling approach.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The document is a multi-chapter OECD report that primarily reviews participation challenges, capacity building, policy dialogue, and descriptive/evidence synthesis rather than estimating a single ML model with an explicitly documented plausible-values (PV) and missing-data strategy. While PISA cognitive outcomes are PV-based in the underlying PISA framework, this report excerpt does not specify how PVs and missing data were handled for any single unified analysis pipeline. Therefore, PV and missing-data handling cannot be attributed to a specific empirical ML procedure from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report is not a single micro-data analysis; it combines (i) interview-based evidence from national project managers, (ii) media-content analysis in selected case-study countries, and (iii) secondary synthesis of OECD PISA 2012 results and related multilevel analyses. For the PISA 2012-based chapter, the excerpt specifies that original analyses focus on 18 middle-income countries participating in PISA 2012 mathematics, with exclusions including Albania and Hungary and excluding certain high-income economies (e.g., China economies such as Hong Kong, Shanghai, Macao) from the analysis set.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report synthesises the experiences of middle-income countries participating in PISA from 2000 to 2015, combining qualitative evidence (interviews with national project managers), descriptive statistics on participation and costs, and secondary evidence from PISA 2012 analyses. It documents financial deterrents (fees, travel, implementation and reporting costs), technical/operational challenges (translation, sampling in decentralised systems, computer-based assessment logistics, coding reliability), and contextual constraints (governance, regulatory environment, press freedom, and cultural factors affecting implementation and dissemination). For education quality and equity, it summarises PISA 2012 mathematics results across 18 middle-income countries and discusses multilevel correlates of performance, including the role of socio-economic background, school climate, instructional time, and opportunities to learn. The report also reviews evidence on how PISA informs policy dialogue, finding limited systematic public media agenda-setting in many middle-income contexts but more consistent use in private dialogue with development partners. Limitations include the lack of a single unified empirical ML pipeline and limited causal attribution of PISA effects on reforms.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction corresponds to an OECD report that is primarily a systematic review/synthesis and descriptive evidence base rather than a single empirical ML study. As a result, there is no single student-level dataset with a unified target variable, ML algorithm, PV-handling specification, or missing-data strategy that can be extracted from the provided text. The report does include references to PISA 2012 multilevel analyses and PV-based outcomes in underlying OECD work, but the excerpt does not provide the complete methodological details needed to populate PV/missing-data fields for a specific ML pipeline.
